stem: Marisol, a collegiate gymnast, started beam imagery eight months ago while she was first learning a new acrobatic series. She images on the beam in the arena where her team competes, wears her competition leotard, runs the images at real-time speed, and includes the nerves she feels at meets. Her script still talks her through each body position one step at a time, although she now performs the series fluidly. She says the imagery feels 'choppy, like I'm learning it all over again.' Using the PETTLEP model, which change should the consultant make?
options: Move her sessions to a quieter gym so that she can focus on each body position
Switch to an external perspective so she can check each body position from outside
Rewrite the script to cue the rhythm and feel of the series as she now performs it
Slow the imagery to half speed so that each part of the series is rehearsed in detail
rationales: Her environment already matches competition because she images in the arena where she competes; moving to a quieter gym would reduce environmental equivalence and wouldn't touch the outdated, step-by-step script she describes.
Perspective is a PETTLEP element, and an external view can help some form-based skills, but her complaint is that the script reflects an earlier stage of learning, not the viewpoint she uses.

PETTLEP's Learning element (Holmes & Collins) says imagery content should be revised as a skill moves from the cognitive toward the autonomous stage; a script that still walks her through each position no longer matches how she performs the series, so it should cue its rhythm and feel instead.
Half-speed imagery breaks PETTLEP's Timing element and would make the images even more piecemeal, the opposite of the fluid performance she now produces.
takeaway: PETTLEP's Learning element: update imagery content as the skill develops so it matches how the performer currently executes it.

stem: Tobias, an elite para swimmer, has excellent technique, but he tells the consultant that his belief in himself 'evaporates' when he sees his main rivals warming up on deck at major meets. He already uses imagery to rehearse his starts and turns. Which imagery content should the consultant help him add to his practice?
options: Seeing himself confident and in control on deck as rivals warm up nearby
Replaying his stroke mechanics in slow motion to refine his catch and kick
Rehearsing the pacing plan he and his coach chose for each length of the race
Picturing himself on the podium receiving a medal at the championship
rationales: Motivational general–mastery imagery—seeing oneself confident, focused, and coping well in challenging situations—is the imagery function most closely linked to self-confidence in the Paivio/Hall framework, and it targets the exact situation in which his confidence drops.
This is cognitive-specific (skill) imagery; his technique is already strong and he already does skill-focused imagery, so it doesn't target his confidence problem.
This is cognitive-general (strategy) imagery; rehearsing a race plan is useful but doesn't address the loss of self-belief triggered by seeing his rivals.
This is motivational-specific (goal) imagery; it can boost motivation, but outcome images don't rehearse staying confident in the situation that undermines him.
takeaway: To build confidence, use motivational general–mastery imagery: rehearse feeling confident and in control in the situations that threaten confidence.

stem: Eleanor, a 61-year-old club golfer, has been saying 'Come on, you've got this!' to herself before every putt. Since she started, her putting stroke has become quick and jerky, and she notices the phrase leaves her feeling 'revved up' over the ball. Based on research matching self-talk to task demands, what change is most appropriate?
options: Keep the phrase but say it on the walk to the green rather than over the ball
Switch to a motivational phrase she writes herself so that it feels more personal
Talk herself through grip, stance, and alignment checks while she stands over the ball
Use one short instructional cue tied to the stroke itself, such as 'pendulum'
rationales: Moving the phrase earlier may soften its effect over the ball, but it is still motivational self-talk for a fine-precision task, and it leaves her with no cue that supports a smooth stroke.
Personally meaningful wording helps self-talk stick, but a motivational phrase of any kind fits effort and power tasks better than a delicate putting stroke.
This is instructional, but a string of checks over the ball overloads attention and pulls her focus inward onto mechanics, which tends to disrupt a well-learned stroke; effective cues are brief.

Research on self-talk (Theodorakis et al.; Hatzigeorgiadis et al.) shows instructional self-talk benefits precision and fine-motor tasks more than motivational self-talk; a single short cue linked to the stroke supports a smooth tempo without the activation her current phrase creates.
takeaway: Match self-talk to the task: instructional cues for precision and technique, motivational cues for effort, strength, and endurance.

stem: Before matches, Kwame, a 16-year-old wrestler, reports a pounding heart, tight shoulders, and nausea. Asked about his thoughts, he says he expects to wrestle well and isn't dwelling on the result; his body 'just goes haywire,' and he feels stiff through the first period. The consultant is choosing a primary technique to teach him. Based on the matching hypothesis, which technique fits best?
options: Reappraisal training so that he reads his pounding heart as a sign he is ready
Progressive muscle relaxation paired with slow breathing in his warm-up
Instructional self-talk cues that keep him focused on his first-period plan
Mastery imagery of wrestling a strong first period with confidence and control
rationales: Reappraising symptoms as facilitative is a useful cognitive strategy, but his physical tension is producing real stiffness, and the matching hypothesis points to a somatic technique for predominantly somatic anxiety.

The matching hypothesis holds that interventions work best when they match the type of anxiety; his symptoms are somatic (racing heart, muscle tension, nausea) with little worry, so somatic techniques such as PMR and slow diaphragmatic breathing fit best.
Instructional cues direct attention, but his problem is bodily tension rather than distraction or a poor game plan, so they don't target the symptoms he describes.
Mastery imagery builds confidence, yet he already feels confident; it doesn't reduce the physiological activation that leaves him stiff.
takeaway: Match the intervention to the anxiety: somatic techniques (PMR, breathing) for bodily symptoms, cognitive techniques for worry—even when another technique sounds appealing.

stem: The performance director of a professional esports team asks the consultant, who is trained in biofeedback, to use heart rate variability (HRV) biofeedback with players who feel 'wired' and rushed during tournament matches. The consultant has explained the rationale, and the players have agreed to participate. Which approach to the first training phase is most consistent with resonance frequency HRV training?
options: Show live HRV during scrimmages and cue players to slow down whenever it drops
Teach players a standard pace of six breaths per minute, then add it to warm-ups
Identify each player's breathing rate that maximizes HRV, then practice it daily
Use heart rate feedback to teach players to lower their resting heart rate
rationales: Feedback during competition-like play is a later transfer step; in the first phase players need to learn the breathing skill under calm conditions before using it under pressure.

Six breaths per minute is close to the typical resonance rate, but resonance frequency training starts by measuring each person's own rate, which varies between individuals, rather than assigning a standard pace.

Resonance frequency HRV biofeedback (Lehrer and colleagues) first identifies the slow breathing rate, typically around 4.5 to 7 breaths per minute, at which each person's HRV is greatest, and then has them practice that rate regularly so the skill can later transfer to performance.
Lowering resting heart rate is a different target; HRV training aims to increase heart rate variability through paced breathing, not to reduce heart rate itself.
takeaway: HRV biofeedback trains slow, paced breathing at each person's resonance frequency (about six breaths per minute), practiced regularly before transfer to performance.

stem: Meera, a collegiate volleyball player, uses a 12-step pre-serve routine that includes bouncing the ball exactly seven times. She has eight seconds to serve after the whistle. When the referee is slow to whistle or an opponent calls a timeout to 'ice' her, she feels thrown off and often misses. What is the best way for the consultant to help her refine the routine?
options: Rehearse the full 12 steps more often in practice so they hold up in matches
Add a refocusing breath she takes before restarting her routine after a delay
Teach her to tune out the referee and opponents by narrowing her focus to the ball
Pare it down to a few core elements, then practice it with delays and timeouts
rationales: More repetitions make the routine more automatic but also more rigid; the problem is that it breaks down when the timing changes, which extra practice of the same fixed sequence won't solve.
A refocusing breath is a useful addition, but she would still be restarting a long, ritualized sequence that depends on exact timing, so the underlying rigidity remains.
Narrowing attention can screen out distractions, but her difficulty is a routine that can't absorb delays, not an inability to ignore the referee or opponents.

Effective pre-performance routines (Cotterill) are built on a few purposeful core elements and are flexible enough to adapt to timing changes; practicing with simulated delays makes the routine robust when matches are disrupted.
takeaway: Effective routines are short, purposeful, flexible, and practiced under realistic disruptions; rigid, ritualistic routines break down when interrupted.

stem: Oskar, a violinist with a professional orchestra, has two featured solo performances next month. At a recent concert, a ringing phone in the audience and a stand light that suddenly flickered each pulled his attention away. He says each distraction lasted only a moment, but he didn't know how to get back into the music and lost several bars. Which strategy should the consultant prioritize in the coming weeks?
options: Write if-then refocusing plans for foreseeable disruptions and rehearse them
Practice the solos with recorded audience noise so that he gets used to distractions
Build a longer pre-performance routine to settle his focus before each solo begins
Teach him a narrow, internal focus on the feel of his bowing to screen out the hall
rationales: Orlick's distraction-control work emphasizes refocusing plans: specific if-then responses for foreseeable disruptions, rehearsed until recovery is quick; this targets his actual problem, which is getting back into the music after a brief distraction.

Exposure to noise can reduce how strongly he reacts, but distractions will still occur, and his difficulty is recovering afterward; practice with noise works best when paired with a plan for refocusing.
A pre-performance routine helps him start the solo focused, but his lapses happened mid-performance, when a routine done beforehand gives him no way back.
An internal focus on bowing pulls attention away from the music and the ensemble, and trying to screen out every stimulus is less realistic than having a quick way to recover.
takeaway: Distractions are inevitable; prepare if-then refocusing plans for foreseeable ones and rehearse them so recovery is quick.

stem: Ramón, a professional relief pitcher, has been trying to 'push away' anxious thoughts on the mound. He reports that the harder he tries not to think about walking batters, the more the thought intrudes and the tighter he feels. The consultant works from a mindfulness-acceptance-commitment (MAC) approach. Which in-session practice best fits this approach?
options: Listing evidence against the thought and writing a more balanced statement
Using a cue word to stop the thought, then shifting to a positive self-statement
Noticing and labeling the thought, then returning his focus to the catcher's glove
Slow diaphragmatic breathing on the mound until the anxious thought fades
rationales: Disputing the thought is cognitive restructuring, a change-based CBT technique; MAC instead changes his relationship to the thought, and arguing with it can keep him engaged with it on the mound.
Thought-stopping is another form of suppression, which tends to produce the rebound he is already experiencing.

MAC (Gardner & Moore) uses mindful awareness and acceptance: he notices and labels the thought without trying to control it and returns attention to task-relevant cues, which avoids the rebound that suppression produces.
Breathing can ease tension, but using it to make the thought go away is still an attempt to control internal experience, which MAC does not aim for.
takeaway: Acceptance-based approaches have athletes notice and allow unwanted thoughts while redirecting attention to the task, rather than suppressing them.

stem: Renata, a regional sales director, tells the consultant her goal for the quarter is 'to be the number-one region in the company.' Two weeks in, she feels anxious each time the company leaderboard updates and says she isn't sure what to do differently day to day. She and the consultant have agreed to strengthen her goal plan. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Keep the ranking goal and add monthly ranking checkpoints so she can track her progress
Work with her manager to set weekly revenue targets that hold her accountable
Teach her a brief breathing routine to use when the leaderboard is updated
Set daily actions she controls, such as client calls, with a weekly action plan
rationales: Monthly ranking checkpoints are still outcome goals that depend on other regions, so they keep her focus on the leaderboard and don't tell her what to do day to day.
Manager-set revenue targets add accountability but remove her ownership and remain largely outcome-based, so they don't clarify the daily actions she controls.
A breathing routine may ease her anxiety in the moment, but she and the consultant agreed to strengthen her goal plan, and the routine doesn't address the missing process goals.

Goal-setting research (Locke & Latham; Kingston & Hardy) supports pairing an outcome goal with controllable process and performance goals; specific behaviors and a weekly action plan give her clear daily direction and reduce her dependence on the leaderboard.
takeaway: Pair outcome goals with specific, controllable process and performance goals and an action plan the client helps build.

stem: The consultant co-led a fire department's live-fire training scenario in which crews practiced a breathing-and-refocus skill under realistic stress. As the drill ends, the training captain suggests closing with a quick summary of 'the right way to do it' so crews can get back to the station. Drawing on experiential learning principles, how should the consultant structure the close of the session?
options: Summarize the key steps of the technique, then hand out a pocket reference card
Guide crews to describe what happened, interpret it, and plan its use on real calls
Have the training captain give each crew feedback on how well it used the skill
Collect brief written ratings from crews so that the drill can be improved
rationales: A summary and reference card are direct instruction; they skip the reflection that experiential learning relies on and leave crews as passive recipients.

Experiential learning (Kolb) moves from concrete experience to reflection, conceptualization, and planned application; a structured debrief has crews describe what happened, interpret it, and plan how they'll use the skill on real calls.
Expert feedback has value, but having the captain evaluate each crew replaces the crews' own reflection and conceptualization, which are the steps that consolidate experiential learning.
Reaction ratings help evaluate the program, but they don't help crews make sense of the experience or plan how to apply the skill.
takeaway: Close experiential training with a structured debrief—what happened, what it means, how it will be applied—rather than a lecture.

stem: The head coach of a girls' U14 club soccer team asks the consultant to help with cohesion because players stick to cliques. The consultant has already observed practices and interviewed players, and can attend only two more sessions this season, while the coach sees the team four times a week. Using Carron and Spink's team-building approach, which plan is likely to be most effective?
options: Train the coach to build distinctiveness, roles, and norms into weekly practices
Use both sessions for consultant-led cohesion activities, then share notes with the coach
Run a team-wide ropes-course outing, then follow up with a group debrief on cliques
Meet with players to explore the cliques further before planning team-building activities
rationales: Carron and Spink's approach is indirect: the consultant teaches the coach, who builds group-environment, group-structure, and group-process strategies into regular practices; with only two consultant sessions, this gets the most frequent and lasting exposure.
Consultant-led activities can help, but two sessions are a low dose, and the coach, who sees the team far more often, would not be equipped to sustain the work.
A one-off outing with a debrief can be memorable, but single events rarely change cohesion over a season, and it doesn't build strategies into the team's routine.
Assessment has value, but the consultant has already observed and interviewed players; more exploration would use up one of the two remaining sessions without starting the intervention.
takeaway: In Carron and Spink's approach, the consultant trains the coach, who builds cohesion through group environment, structure, and process strategies.

stem: Yuki, a 15-year-old figure skater, uses imagery to rehearse her free skate. She mentions that her imagery takes nearly twice as long as the real program because she 'goes slowly to get every detail right.' Her coach's main concern is that her jumps feel rushed and off-rhythm in competition. Following the PETTLEP model, what should the consultant recommend?
options: Add her program music to the slow imagery so that she hears each musical cue
Image the program at real-time speed, slowing down only isolated elements
Add the arena's sights and sounds so that the imagery feels like competition
Switch to an external perspective so she can check the rhythm of each jump
rationales: Music would add a useful cue, but playing it alongside slowed imagery mismatches the real tempo and may reinforce the timing problem.

PETTLEP's Timing element (Holmes & Collins) calls for imagery at the same speed as actual performance; rehearsing at real speed builds the rhythm her jumps lack, and slow motion can still be used briefly for specific technical elements.
Environmental detail supports PETTLEP's Environment element, but her images would still run at half speed, leaving the timing mismatch in place.
Perspective is a separate PETTLEP choice; changing her viewpoint doesn't fix imagery that runs far slower than the program.
takeaway: PETTLEP's Timing element: image skills at real-time speed, using slow motion only selectively.

stem: An elite women's rugby sevens squad is installing three new restart plays one week before an international tournament. The head coach wants players to mentally rehearse where to run and which option to take on each call without adding physical training load. Which type of imagery should the consultant emphasize with the squad?
options: Motivational general–arousal imagery to energize players for each restart
Cognitive-specific imagery of each player's passing and catching technique
Motivational general–mastery imagery of staying composed on each restart call
Cognitive-general imagery of the movement patterns and choices in each play
rationales: Arousal imagery regulates activation, but the coach's goal is learning the plays, not energizing players.
Cognitive-specific imagery targets individual skills; the need here is team strategy and decision-making, not passing technique.
Mastery imagery builds confidence and composure, which can help in a tournament, but it doesn't help players learn where to run and which option to take on the new plays.

In Paivio's framework (and Hall's SIQ), cognitive-general imagery rehearses strategies, game plans, and routines; it lets players learn the movement and decision patterns of the new plays without adding physical load.
takeaway: Use cognitive-general imagery for strategies and game plans; cognitive-specific imagery for individual skills.

stem: Jonah, a soldier preparing for a special operations selection course, reports that in the final miles of long loaded ruck marches his self-talk drifts to 'I can't keep this up,' and his pace drops. His technique and route planning are not the issue; the challenge is sustaining effort through fatigue. Which self-talk approach should the consultant help him practice?
options: Short motivational statements he chooses, rehearsed during training marches
Instructional cues about posture and stride that he repeats during hard miles
Dissociative strategies, such as counting steps, to take his mind off fatigue
Saying 'stop' when the thought appears, then clearing his mind of it
rationales: Self-talk research (Hatzigeorgiadis et al.; Theodorakis et al.) shows motivational self-talk benefits endurance and effort tasks; statements he chooses and rehearses in training are more meaningful and more likely to be available when he is fatigued.
Instructional self-talk suits technique and precision tasks; the stem states that technique is not the issue.
Dissociation can ease perceived exertion for some people, but it doesn't replace the negative self-talk he reports or give him statements that sustain effort.
Thought-stopping tries to suppress the thought without replacing it, has weaker support than matched self-talk, and can leave a gap that the negative thought fills again.
takeaway: For endurance and effort tasks, use motivational self-talk the performer owns and has practiced in training.

stem: Gabriel, a startup founder, will pitch to investors next month. He says his body feels calm and loose when he rehearses, and his practice pitches go well. In the days before a pitch, however, he lies awake replaying worst-case questions and predicting that investors will dismiss him. Applying the matching hypothesis, which technique should the consultant emphasize?
options: Progressive muscle relaxation each night to help him wind down before pitches
Biofeedback training to lower his heart rate during rehearsal pitches
Identifying his catastrophic predictions and testing them against evidence
Slow diaphragmatic breathing practiced at bedtime in the days before a pitch
rationales: PMR is a somatic technique; his body is already calm and loose, so it doesn't target the worry that keeps him awake.
Heart rate biofeedback reduces physiological arousal, but his rehearsals already go well physically; his problem is cognitive.

The matching hypothesis says cognitive anxiety responds best to cognitive techniques; his symptoms are rumination and catastrophic predictions, so cognitive restructuring that tests and reframes those predictions fits best.
Breathing is a somatic technique; it may help him relax at night but doesn't address the catastrophic thinking behind his anxiety.
takeaway: Cognitive anxiety calls for cognitive techniques (e.g., restructuring); somatic anxiety calls for somatic techniques.

stem: A county EMS agency asks the consultant to teach paramedics a breathing technique for staying composed at chaotic scenes. In the first workshop, several medics say they tried slow breathing once during a cardiac arrest call and 'it didn't do anything.' None has practiced it since. What is the most appropriate way to structure the next phase of training?
options: Practice it daily in calm settings, then rehearse it in simulated high-stress calls
Switch to a box-breathing pattern with a count that is easier to recall under stress
Add a guided breathing session at the start of each shift to lower baseline stress
Explain the physiology of slow breathing, then ask medics to try it on their next calls
rationales: Arousal-regulation skills must be overlearned before they work under pressure: daily practice in calm conditions, then graded rehearsal in realistic simulations, lets the skill transfer to chaotic scenes.

Box breathing is a legitimate technique, but switching methods assumes the first one failed; a single untrained attempt under extreme stress says little about the technique, and any new one would fail the same way without practice.
A start-of-shift session may lower general stress, but it doesn't build a skill medics can use at a chaotic scene or rehearse it under stress.
Understanding the rationale can increase buy-in, but asking medics to try it again on real calls without practice repeats the conditions that produced the failed attempt.
takeaway: Teach breathing as a skill: overlearn it in calm conditions, then rehearse it under progressively realistic stress.

stem: Paloma, a 17-year-old tennis player, often loses several points in a row after an unforced error because she is still replaying the mistake as the next point starts. She has about 20 seconds between points. Which between-point strategy should the consultant help her develop?
options: Note a quick technical correction, then replay the corrected shot in her mind
Take extra time between points so that she can slow her breathing and heart rate
A short routine to let go of the error, reset her breathing, and plan the point
Jot down her errors at changeovers so she can review them with her coach later
rationales: A quick correction can be part of some routines, but replaying the shot keeps her attention on the error she can't let go of, which is the problem she has.
Using her full time can help, but calming her body doesn't address the mental replaying, and the rules limit how long she can take.

Between-point routines (e.g., respond, relax, prepare, ritual) help players release the previous point, recover physically, and refocus on a plan for the next one, which directly addresses her carryover from errors.
Reviewing errors after the match supports learning, but writing them down during play keeps her focused on mistakes and does nothing to reset her before the next point.
takeaway: Between-play routines help performers release the last play, recover, and refocus on the next one.

stem: Zuri, a professional soccer goalkeeper, sometimes concedes goals after long spells when play is in the opposing half. She says her mind drifts to the crowd or to mistakes she made earlier, and she is 'late to read' an attack when it suddenly develops. Using Nideffer's model of attention, what should the consultant help her build?
options: A habit of holding a narrow focus on the ball whenever it is in the opposing half
A broad-internal review of the opponents' attacking patterns during quiet spells
A centering breath at each stoppage to clear her mind of the mistakes she made earlier
Cue words to hold a broad external scan in quiet spells, narrowing as attacks build
rationales: A sustained narrow focus is tiring and misses the broad picture of player positions that a goalkeeper needs to read a developing attack.
Broad-internal analysis suits planning, but doing it during open play turns her attention inward, which is exactly why she is late to read attacks.
Centering helps her reset at stoppages, but her lapses happen during long spells of open play, when she needs to stay externally engaged with the game.

Nideffer's model describes attention by width and direction and stresses shifting to match demands; cue words help her hold a broad-external scan of the field during quiet spells, which keeps her out of internal drift, and then narrow onto the ball and attackers as play approaches.
takeaway: Train planned attentional shifts—broad to narrow, internal to external—with cue words tied to game situations, including quiet spells.

stem: Anouk, a corps de ballet dancer, has not auditioned for a soloist role in two seasons because she fears 'freezing' in front of the artistic director. In earlier sessions she clearly named dancing expressively for an audience as what matters most in her career, and an audition opens in six weeks. The consultant is using an acceptance and commitment approach. Which next step best fits this approach?
options: Use cognitive restructuring to weaken her fear of freezing, then set an audition date
Agree with her on entering the audition, practicing willingness to feel the fear
Explore what expressive dancing means to her in more depth before setting goals
Teach her a relaxation routine to calm the fear so that it stops blocking her
rationales: Restructuring is a change-based CBT strategy, and making the audition wait until fear is reduced is the kind of control agenda ACT asks clients to let go of.

ACT links valued directions to committed action; because she has already named what matters, the next step is a concrete commitment, entering the audition, while practicing willingness to have fear and other difficult internal experiences.
Values clarification is part of ACT, but she has already identified her value clearly; more exploration delays the committed action the six-week window allows.
Relaxation used to make fear go away is an emotional-control strategy; ACT aims for action alongside fear rather than its removal.
takeaway: In ACT, clients take values-guided action while making room for difficult feelings, rather than waiting for fear to disappear.

stem: A consultant helped Daniel, a collegiate swimmer, set three specific process goals for practice, such as holding a tight streamline off every wall. A month later, Daniel says he 'kind of forgot about them' and isn't sure whether he is improving. He and his coach both still believe the goals are the right ones. What should the consultant do next?
options: Revisit the goals with him and set new ones that he finds more engaging
Ask the coach to remind him of the goals at the start of each practice
Set up a simple log with him and review his progress briefly each week
Add a season outcome goal, such as a qualifying time, to give the goals more drive
rationales: He, his coach, and the consultant all agree the goals are right; changing them doesn't fix the missing feedback that made them fade.
Reminders keep the goals in view, but they give him no information about whether he is progressing, which is what he says is missing.
Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham) identifies feedback as essential for goals to affect performance; a tracking log and brief weekly reviews keep the goals salient and show him his progress.
An outcome goal may add motivation, but it doesn't provide the ongoing feedback on his process goals that he lacks.
takeaway: Goals work only with feedback: build in self-monitoring and regular progress reviews.

stem: A national wheelchair rugby program asks the consultant to deliver a four-session focus skills workshop by video call because athletes live in different cities. In the first session, a 60-minute slide presentation, most cameras went off and few athletes spoke. How should the consultant adapt the remaining sessions?
options: Keep the slides but shorten the talk and add a question period at the end
Ask athletes to keep cameras on, then call on them by name to share examples
Send short recorded lessons to watch beforehand, then use calls for questions
Break sessions into short segments with breakout practice, polls, and a debrief
rationales: A shorter talk helps, but the format stays mostly passive, and a question period at the end gives athletes no chance to practice the focus skills.
Requiring cameras and calling on people can feel coercive and doesn't make the content more engaging; participation tends to improve when the design is interactive.
Pre-recorded lessons can free up live time, but using calls only for questions still leaves no structured practice of the skills.

Effective virtual delivery uses short content blocks, active practice (e.g., breakout rooms), interactive tools such as polls, and debriefs, applying experiential learning principles that keep participants engaged and help skills transfer.
takeaway: In virtual delivery, keep segments short and build in active practice, interaction, and debriefing.

stem: Midway through the season, players on a collegiate men's lacrosse team argue in film sessions about who should slide to an open dodger, and several reserves have stopped engaging at practice, telling the consultant they don't see how they contribute. The coaching staff agrees to a team-building intervention. Within Carron and Spink's framework, which focus best targets these problems?
options: Group structure: clarifying each player's role and building acceptance of it
Group structure: setting team norms for communication and effort at practice
Group processes: setting shared team goals that every player helps to create
Group environment: increasing time together through team meals and travel
rationales: The arguments about defensive responsibilities show role ambiguity, and the disengaged reserves show low role acceptance; Carron and Spink place role clarity and role acceptance under group structure.
Norms are also a group-structure strategy, and better communication norms might reduce arguing, but they don't resolve who is responsible for what or help reserves see their contribution.
Shared goals are a group-process strategy that can build commitment, but they don't define individual responsibilities on the field or address how reserves understand their part.
Proximity is a group-environment strategy that can increase interaction, but more time together doesn't clarify responsibilities or build acceptance of limited playing time.
takeaway: Confusion about responsibilities and resentment of one's part on the team call for group-structure strategies: clarify roles and build role acceptance.

stem: Valentina, an elite karate athlete, competes in kata, where judges score the form, shape, and precision of her movements. She uses imagery only from an internal perspective, 'through my own eyes,' and wants imagery to help her refine the body lines the judges see. Which adjustment is best supported by imagery research?
options: Add detailed kinesthetic cues to her internal imagery to sharpen the feel of each stance
Slow her internal imagery so she can examine each movement before real-time runs
Watch video of top kata athletes in place of part of her imagery practice
Add external-perspective imagery of her form while keeping the feel of each move
rationales: Kinesthetic detail is valuable, but staying with an internal view alone gives her no visual information about the body lines the judges score.
Slow-motion imagery can help examine technique, but it keeps her internal viewpoint, so it doesn't let her see her form, and it departs from real-time timing.
Observing skilled performers helps learning, but it shows other athletes' form rather than her own, and replacing imagery with video doesn't improve how she images.

Imagery research (e.g., Hardy and colleagues) suggests external visual imagery benefits form-based skills in which body shape matters, and kinesthetic imagery can be combined with either visual perspective; PETTLEP likewise treats perspective as a choice matched to the task.
takeaway: Match imagery perspective to the task: external visual imagery helps form-based skills, and kinesthetic feel can accompany either perspective.

stem: During guided imagery, Brianna, a 16-year-old softball pitcher, keeps 'seeing' her pitches sail high even when she tries to picture them hitting the catcher's mitt. She is growing frustrated and says imagery 'just makes it worse.' What is the most appropriate way for the consultant to proceed?
options: Pause imagery and show her video of her own good pitches to rebuild confidence
Have her stop, rewind, and replay the image correctly, starting with simple scenes
Switch her to an external perspective so she can watch the pitch path from outside
Lead a relaxation exercise first, then return to the same full pitching scenes
rationales: Video of successful pitches can support confidence and can complement imagery, but pausing imagery doesn't build the controllability she lacks.

Controllability is a trainable imagery skill: stopping, rewinding, and replaying the image correctly, starting with simple, easy-to-control scenes and progressing gradually, builds control; slow-motion replays or pairing imagery with physical rehearsal or video can also help.
Changing perspective doesn't give her more control over the image; the errant pitch would likely appear from either viewpoint.
Relaxation before imagery can improve focus, but returning to the same complex scenes without a strategy for correcting the image leaves the control problem unaddressed.
takeaway: When images go wrong, stop, rewind, and replay correctly, and build controllability with simple scenes first.

stem: Lucan, a wheelchair basketball player on a national development squad, says his imagery of free throws is 'like watching a silent movie—I see it, but I don't feel anything.' The consultant's current script describes only what he would see on the court. Which revision to the script is most likely to help?
options: Add his physical and emotional responses, like arm drive and quiet confidence
Add more visual detail about the arena's lighting, signage, and crowd
Add his coach's spoken reminders about elbow position at each step of the shot
Record the script in his own voice so that it sounds more familiar and personal
rationales: Lang's bioinformational theory and PETTLEP both emphasize response propositions—physical and emotional reactions—not just stimulus details; adding sensations such as arm drive and feelings such as quiet confidence makes imagery more vivid and functionally equivalent.
More visual detail adds stimulus propositions, but his script already describes what he sees; he lacks the feel of the shot.
Technical reminders add auditory content but describe what to do rather than what he feels, so the imagery would still lack bodily and emotional sensation.
A familiar voice can make a recording more engaging, but if the script still describes only what he sees, he will still feel nothing.
takeaway: Effective imagery scripts include response propositions—what the performer feels physically and emotionally—not just what they see.

stem: Before every competition, Arlo, a 15-year-old diver, tells himself, 'I always mess up my reverse dive at big meets.' His meet records show he has performed it cleanly in four of his last six meets. Arlo and the consultant have agreed to work on this self-talk. Which approach best reflects cognitive restructuring?
options: Replace it with an affirmation he repeats, such as 'I nail my reverse dive'
Say 'stop' when the thought appears, then shift to a cue about his takeoff
Compare the thought with his meet records and write a realistic replacement
Notice the thought and let it pass without arguing with it, then step up to dive
rationales: An affirmation he doesn't yet believe skips the evaluation step; restructuring tests the original thought first so the replacement is credible.
Thought-stopping with a task cue interrupts the thought but doesn't examine or change the belief behind it.
Cognitive restructuring identifies an unhelpful thought, evaluates it against evidence—here, four clean dives in six meets—and replaces it with a realistic, constructive statement (Beck).
This is cognitive defusion, an acceptance-based technique; it changes his relationship to the thought rather than testing its content, so it isn't restructuring.
takeaway: Restructuring tests unhelpful thoughts against evidence and replaces them with realistic, constructive statements.

stem: The consultant gave Ines, a collegiate high jumper, the cue word 'focus' to use during her approach. After two weeks, she reports that it 'doesn't really mean anything' to her. Her coach says her main technical fault is cutting the curve of her approach too early. What is the best next step?
options: Invite her to pick a motivational cue, such as 'explode,' to energize her approach
Work with her and her coach on a short cue for running the full curve, like 'lean in'
Have her coach call out a cue from the apron as she enters the curve on each jump
Give her three technical cues covering the approach, plant, and takeoff to rotate
rationales: Her own choice of wording helps, but a motivational cue targets effort rather than the technical fault her coach identified.
Effective cue words are brief, personally meaningful, and tied to the key task element; developing one with her and her coach targets the curve fault and gives her ownership.
Coach prompts can help during learning, but they create reliance on external cues and don't give her self-talk she can use in competition.
Several rotating cues overload attention during a fast approach and dilute focus on the one fault that matters most.
takeaway: Develop cue words with the performer: brief, personally meaningful, and tied to the key task element.

stem: Over six weeks, the consultant has taught Odalys, a professional opera singer, full progressive muscle relaxation: tensing and releasing 16 muscle groups in a 25-minute session. She can now relax deeply at home but says she can't do 'all of that' backstage between scenes. What is the most appropriate next step in her training?
options: Move to shorter forms: fewer muscle groups, release-only, and a cue word
Switch to slow breathing backstage and keep full PMR as her home practice
Record a 10-minute PMR script that she can play on headphones in the wings
Do the full session in her dressing room before the show, then rely on its carryover
rationales: PMR is designed to progress from full tense–release practice to abbreviated forms (fewer muscle groups, release-only, then cue-controlled relaxation) so the skill can be used in seconds during performance (Jacobson; later applied adaptations).
Breathing is useful, but abandoning her PMR progression wastes six weeks of skill-building that can be condensed into a backstage tool.
A shorter recording is still too long and equipment-dependent for the brief gaps between scenes, and it skips the cue-controlled stage.
Relaxation before the show fades over a long performance, and she still has no brief tool for the moments between scenes.
takeaway: Progress PMR from full tense–release sessions to abbreviated, release-only, and cue-controlled forms usable in performance.

stem: After eight weeks of HRV biofeedback, Fergus, a professional golfer, reliably produces a smooth, high-amplitude heart rhythm while watching the screen during office sessions. On the course, he says he 'can't get there' without the display in front of him. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Have him wear a heart-rate monitor on the course and check it between shots
Add more office sessions with the display, then retest him on the course
Teach him a different self-regulation skill that doesn't rely on equipment
Fade the display during sessions, then practice the breathing on the course
rationales: Checking a monitor between shots keeps him dependent on external feedback and adds a distraction during play.
More sessions with constant feedback strengthen the skill only while he sees the display, which is the dependency he already shows.
The skill he has learned is sound; it simply hasn't been transferred, so starting over wastes eight weeks of progress.

Biofeedback is meant as temporary scaffolding: gradually fading the display builds internal awareness of the target state, and practicing the paced breathing on the course supports transfer to performance (Lehrer and colleagues).
takeaway: Biofeedback is scaffolding: fade the display so the self-regulation skill transfers to performance.

stem: A professional women's basketball team's free-throw percentage drops late in close games. With the players' agreement, the performance staff recorded eye tracking during pressured free-throw drills and found that the less accurate shooters glance between the backboard, the ball, and the hoop, settling their gaze on a target only briefly before they release. Which training approach do these findings most directly support?
options: Add graded pressure to free-throw practice while players keep their current routine
Lengthen a steady final gaze on one precise spot before and through the release
Teach instructional self-talk about elbow alignment for players to use at the line
Have players image successful free throws from an external perspective before games
rationales: Pressure training helps performers adapt to stress, but the data point to a specific gaze-control problem that practicing under pressure with the same routine wouldn't correct.

The quiet eye (Vickers) is the final fixation on a target before movement begins; longer, steadier quiet eye periods distinguish accurate shooters and are more robust under pressure, and quiet eye training has improved free-throw accuracy, so the gaze findings point directly to it.
A technical cue can help mechanics, but it doesn't change where or how long players look, and an inward focus on mechanics can disrupt a well-learned skill under pressure.
Imagery may build confidence and rehearse the shot, but it doesn't train the visual attention problem the eye tracking revealed.
takeaway: When gaze data show a brief, unstable final fixation in an aiming task, quiet eye training is the targeted intervention.

stem: Eli, a 12-year-old BMX racer, says that once he rolls into the start gate, his legs feel shaky, his thoughts jump to the riders beside him, and he is often late out of the gate. He has only a few seconds between setting his pedal and the start cadence. Which technique best fits this situation?
options: A short muscle-relaxation sequence he runs through while he waits in the gate
Imagery of the whole lap, from the gate drop to the finish, before each moto
A one-breath centering routine that ends on a start cue word, such as 'snap'
Counting his breaths slowly so that his mind stays off the riders beside him
rationales: Muscle relaxation can ease tension, but even a short sequence takes longer than the few seconds he has and doesn't direct his attention to the start.
Imagery before the moto can help preparation, but it happens away from the gate and doesn't give him a tool for the shaky legs and drifting thoughts he feels once he is in it.

Centering (Nideffer) is a brief technique: one slow diaphragmatic breath with attention on the body's center, which releases tension, followed by a task-relevant cue that narrows attention onto the start; it fits his few seconds and targets both his physical and attentional symptoms.
Counting breaths may calm him and keep his mind off rivals, but it leaves his attention on counting rather than on the cadence and the start.
takeaway: Centering combines one calming breath with a task-relevant cue, making it suited to brief windows before explosive actions.

stem: The director of a national swimming academy for 15- to 18-year-olds asks the consultant to help coaches 'build resilience' in their swimmers. Some coaches believe the best way is to criticize swimmers harshly and withhold reassurance so they 'toughen up.' Which recommendation is most consistent with research on developing resilience in performers?
options: Help coaches cut back criticism and focus feedback on praise so swimmers feel secure
Raise challenge in steps while coaches give strong support and debrief setbacks
Keep the coaches' current style, and teach swimmers coping skills in workshops
Set tougher sets and race simulations, with coaches stepping back so swimmers cope alone
rationales: High support with little challenge creates a comfortable environment; swimmers may feel secure but won't develop the resilience that comes from facing demands.

Fletcher and Sarkar's work on resilience points to a facilitative environment that combines high challenge with high support, plus reflection on setbacks, so performers grow from adversity rather than being overwhelmed or sheltered.
Coping skills help, but teaching them while keeping a harsh, unsupportive climate leaves the environment that shapes resilience unchanged.
High challenge with little support creates an unrelenting environment, which tends to produce stress and burnout rather than resilience.
takeaway: Resilience grows in environments that combine high challenge with high support and reflection—not harshness, overprotection, or challenge without support.

stem: Five days before the conference tournament, a collegiate men's basketball coach asks the consultant to introduce a new six-session mindfulness program to the team. The players have used a simple breathing-and-refocus routine all season and say it helps them. What is the best response?
options: Deliver the six sessions in condensed form across this week's practices
Offer the program this week as optional sessions for players who want extra tools
Ask the players to vote on whether to start the program before the tournament
Keep the current routine for the tournament and start the program in the off-season
rationales: Condensing a new program into the week before a major event gives players no time to learn it and risks disrupting the routine they trust.
Optional sessions sound low-risk, but they still introduce a new skill set right before the tournament, when attention should go to what players already use well.
Seeking players' input is good practice, but putting the timing to a vote shifts a professional judgment onto them and may still lead to new skills being introduced at the worst time.

New mental skills are best introduced in the off-season or preseason, when there's time to learn and practice them; close to major competition, consultants reinforce familiar skills that already work.
takeaway: Teach new mental skills in the off-season or preseason; near major competition, reinforce what athletes already know.

stem: A recreational youth hockey association asks the consultant to teach relaxation skills to a group of 8- to 10-year-old players, many of whom find it hard to sit still for long, in a single 30-minute session at the rink. Coaches and several parents will watch. Which delivery approach best fits this group's developmental level?
options: A brief talk on how stress affects the body, then a 10-minute guided relaxation
A shortened muscle-relaxation script read calmly while players lie still on mats
Brief games, such as 'robot and spaghetti' muscles and balloon breathing
Simple relaxation goals plus a practice log for home that parents sign each night
rationales: Even a brief explanation of stress physiology is abstract for this age, and a 10-minute passive exercise is long for restless young children.
Shortening the script helps, but lying still while listening is passive and hard for children who struggle to sit still.

Children this age learn best through brief, concrete, playful activities; contrasting tense 'robot' and loose 'spaghetti' muscles and using balloon breathing make relaxation tangible and keep them engaged.
Home practice and parent involvement can support learning later, but goal-setting and logs are not the best use of a single session with young children who first need to experience the skill.
takeaway: Adapt delivery to the population: young children need brief, concrete, playful activities.

stem: With a collegiate soccer player's consent, the consultant is coordinating with the athletic trainer who oversees her ACL rehabilitation. She has already learned a breathing-and-cue relaxation skill with the consultant. The athletic trainer notices that she tenses and holds her breath during painful range-of-motion exercises. What is the best way for the consultant to support the rehabilitation sessions?
options: Attend her rehabilitation sessions for now to cue the skill during painful exercises
Suggest that the athletic trainer adjust the exercises to reduce her pain
Brief the athletic trainer on her cue so the trainer can prompt it during exercises
Teach her a healing imagery skill to use at home between rehabilitation sessions
rationales: Attending sessions is resource-intensive and hard to sustain; the athletic trainer is already present at every session and is better placed to prompt the skill.
Modifying exercises is a clinical decision for the athletic trainer and medical team, outside the consultant's role.

Extending mental skills through stakeholders who are present—here the athletic trainer, with the athlete's consent—supports transfer of a skill she already has while each professional stays within role.
Healing imagery may support recovery, but it doesn't address the breath-holding and tension that occur during the exercises themselves.
takeaway: Extend mental skills through stakeholders, such as athletic trainers, while each professional stays within role.

stem: During the second session of a mindfulness program for a company's leadership team, several executives say they are 'failing' because their minds keep wandering to email during the breathing practice. Some suggest dropping the practice altogether. How should the consultant respond during the debrief?
options: Shorten the practice to two minutes so their minds have less time to wander
Explain that noticing the wandering and coming back is the practice itself
Suggest they clear their inboxes before each session to remove the distraction
Invite them to try a guided body scan instead, since it gives the mind more to do
rationales: Shorter practices can help beginners, but cutting time to avoid wandering treats wandering as failure, the misunderstanding that is discouraging them.
In mindfulness training (Kabat-Zinn), noticing that the mind has wandered and gently returning to the anchor is the core skill; normalizing this reframes their 'failure' as successful practice.
Clearing inboxes may reduce one trigger, but minds wander regardless, and the suggestion implies wandering is a problem to eliminate.
A body scan is a valid mindfulness practice, but switching techniques implies wandering means the method is failing; the mind will wander in any practice.
takeaway: In mindfulness practice, noticing the mind has wandered and returning to the anchor is the skill being trained.

stem: In Carron and Spink's team-building framework, giving an exercise class its own group name, matching shirts, and slogan posters on the studio wall are strategies that primarily target which component of the framework?
options: Group environment, by fostering the group's distinctiveness
Group processes, by increasing cooperation and communication among members
Group structure, by clarifying members' roles and the group's norms
Group goals, by setting shared attendance targets for the class
rationales: Carron and Spink's framework places distinctiveness strategies—a group name, shirts, slogans—under group environment, an input that contributes to cohesion through group structure and group processes.
Group processes involve sacrifice, interaction, and communication; a name, shirts, and slogans don't primarily target these.
Group structure covers roles, norms, and leadership; the strategies described don't change roles or norms.
Goals are not a separate component in Carron and Spink's framework; goal setting sits under group processes, and the strategies described set no goals—they create a distinctive shared identity.
takeaway: Carron and Spink: group environment (distinctiveness, proximity) and group structure (roles, norms) feed group processes (goals, sacrifice, communication) that build cohesion.
